newsitem.title: JAPAN: Yachting-Aussie beefs Up Nippon Challenge.
newsitem.headline: Yachting-Aussie beefs Up Nippon Challenge.

text.p: Stung by two disappointing America's Cup appearances, Japan has turned to veteran Australian yachtsman Peter Gilmour to lead its next challenge for the prize.
Japan not only wants the cup but hopes a win might also revive its own proud seafaring tradition.

The chairman of the Nippon Challenge America's Cup 2000 syndicate, Tatsumitsu Yamasaki, believes that wanting to win the competition on behalf of his nation, no matter the cost, is natural - "part of being human."
Both in 1992, when the cup stayed in the United States and in 1995, when it went to New Zealand, Japan never came close to seeing it filled with sake.
However, the arrival in town of Gilmour, one of the world's best match-racing sailors, is sending an optimistic ripple through Japan.
"I know Japan can win, given the boat and technology to hand, the syndicate back-up and enthusiasm, and the potential of my crew," Gilmour told Reuters in a recent interview.
"Getting my 15 other shipmates to realise this and bring it all together is half my battle at sea."
Gilmour's Australian nationality is no bar to leading Japan because under rule changes he can head the challenge if he has lived in Japan for three years before the race.
The America's Cup is an event won just as much on land as on water, and Gilmour believes Japan may have a headstart through its technology.
Behind the exhilarating days when the crews actually race are months and years of measuring, training, fund-raising, refining and researching.
It is a sport which needs workaholics in the backroom and heroes out front on the bridge.
"I haven't come here to make the team do things my way. Rather I've arrived in order to hone Japanese sailing strengths and help them reach winning form," Gilmour said.
Respecting the culture and getting along well with his crew is the key to Gilmour's approach.
"How else can I learn the psychology of all the members and feel how to blend them all together? I must know my crew as they are and as they can be."
In 1995, he coached the Japanese challengers and "individual spontaneity was lacking."
"We can prepare quite well for the expected, but the unexpected also needs tackling," he said.
Gilmour hopes that Japanese technological ingenuity will make up for lack of experience in the early days of the cup.

"Research is a difficult game of balance. For security, our cards are played close to our chest and at the same time we must show what we've got in order to get other professional feedback. Mistakes can occur if you're overcautious."
Right now, a professor at Tokyo University is busy making waves in test tanks and computers.

"Although we're trying to finalise the design and hardware for the Auckland races, we're also keeping our options open so as to include any new vital developments over the next three years. We may regret it later if we finally make up our minds now."
All entrants for the America's Cup used to be 12-metre boats with a crew of 11, averaging about 60 feet in length and needing winds of at least 20 knots to reach top speeds of more than 12 knots.

The current "F1" ocean racer is the longer and lighter IACC (International America's Cup Class) with a keel of 22 tons, a two-ton hull and a one-ton mast. The extra sailpower for bringing top knots from slower winds needs five more crew.

But as Gilmour pointed out: "Racing is mainly a battle between not enough wind and too much. Getting rid of excess energy from the wind is vital before it causes too much stress on the rigging and masts."
If Japan wins the cup in 2000, one thing is certain, according to syndicate leader Yamasaki: "Japan will become a nation of seafarers again and that's even better than winning the cup."
